content.heading: 5.6 Discrete Dynamical Systems
content.paragraph: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors provide the key to understanding the long-term behavior, or evolution, of a dynamical system described by a difference equation $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$. Such an equation was used to model population movement in Section 1.10, and will be used in various Markov chains in Section 5.9 and the spotted owl population in the introductory example for this chapter. The vectors $\textbf{x}_{k}$ give information about the system as time (denoted by $k$) passes, where $k$ is a nonnegative integer. In the spotted owl example, for instance, $\textbf{x}_{k}$ listed the numbers of owls in three age classes at time $k$.

The applications in this section focus on ecological problems because they are easier to state and explain than, say, problems in physics or engineering. However, dynamical systems arise in many scientific fields. For instance, standard undergraduate courses in control systems discuss several aspects of dynamical systems. The modern state-space design method in such courses relies heavily on matrix algebra.1 The steady-state response of a control system is the engineering equivalent of what we call here the “long-term behavior” of the dynamical system $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$.

Until Example 6, we assume that $A$ is diagonalizable, with $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$, and corresponding eigenvalues, $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$. For convenience, assume the eigenvectors are arranged so that $|\text{λ}_{1}| \geq |\text{λ}_{2}| \geq \cdots \geq |\text{λ}_{n}|$. Since $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$ is a basis for $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$, any initial vector $\textbf{x}_{0}$ can be written uniquely as

content.heading: A Predator–Prey System
content.paragraph: Deep in the redwood forests of California, dusky-footed wood rats provide up to $80\%$ of the diet for the spotted owl, the main predator of the wood rat. Example 1 uses a linear dynamical system to model the physical system of the owls and the rats. (Admittedly, the model is unrealistic in several respects, but it can provide a starting point for the study of more complicated nonlinear models used by environmental scientists.)

content.heading: Graphical Description of Solutions
content.paragraph: When $A$ is $2 \times 2$, algebraic calculations can be supplemented by a geometric description of a system’s evolution. We can view the equation $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ as a description of what happens to an initial point $\textbf{x}_{0}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{2}$ as it is transformed repeatedly by the mapping $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! A\textbf{x}$. The graph of $\textbf{x}_{0},\textbf{x}_{1},\ldots$ is called a trajectory of the dynamical system.

content.paragraph: In Example 2, the origin is called an attractor of the dynamical system because all trajectories tend toward $\textbf{0}$. This occurs whenever both eigenvalues are less than 1 in magnitude. The direction of greatest attraction is along the line through $\textbf{0}$ and the eigenvector $\textbf{v}_{2}$ for the eigenvalue of smaller magnitude.

In the next example, both eigenvalues of $A$ are larger than $1$ in magnitude, and 0 is called a repeller of the dynamical system. All solutions of $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ except the (constant) zero solution are unbounded and tend away from the origin.2

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Both terms grow in size, but the first term grows faster. So the direction of greatest repulsion is the line through $\textbf{0}$ and the eigenvector for the eigenvalue of larger magnitude. Figure 2 shows several trajectories that begin at points quite close to $\textbf{0}$.

image.alt: A graph shows the origin as a repeller with various lines and curves pointing away from the origin. Many points trace the lines and the curves.

content.paragraph: In the next example, $\textbf{0}$ is called a saddle point because the origin attracts solutions from some directions and repels them in other directions. This occurs whenever one eigenvalue is greater than $1$ in magnitude and the other is less than $1$ in magnitude. The direction of greatest attraction is determined by an eigenvector for the eigenvalue of smaller magnitude. The direction of greatest repulsion is determined by an eigenvector for the eigenvalue of greater magnitude.

If we write $\textbf{y}_{k}$ as $\textbf{y}(k)$ and denote the entries in $\textbf{y}(k)$ by $y_{1}(k),\ldots,y_{n}(k)$, then

The change of variable from $\textbf{x}_{k}$ to $\textbf{y}_{k}$ has decoupled the system of difference equations. The evolution of $y_{1}(k)$, for example, is unaffected by what happens to $y_{2}(k),\ldots,y_{n}(k)$, because $y_{1}(k + 1) = \text{λ}_{1} \cdot y_{1}(k)$ for each $k$.

The equation $\textbf{x}_{k} = P\textbf{y}_{k}$ says that $\textbf{y}_{k}$ is the coordinate vector of $\textbf{x}_{k}$ with respect to the eigenvector basis $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$. We can decouple the system $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ by making calculations in the new eigenvector coordinate system. When $n = 2$, this amounts to using graph paper with axes in the directions of the two eigenvectors.

content.heading: Complex Eigenvalues
content.paragraph: When a real $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has complex eigenvalues, $A$ is not diagonalizable (when acting on $\textbf{ℝ}^{2}$), but the dynamical system $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ is easy to describe. Example 3 of Section 5.5 illustrated the case in which the eigenvalues have absolute value $1$. The iterates of a point $\textbf{x}_{0}$ spiral around the origin along an elliptical trajectory.

If $A$ has two complex eigenvalues whose absolute value is greater than $1$, then $\textbf{0}$ is a repeller and iterates of $\textbf{x}_{0}$ will spiral outward around the origin. If the absolute values of the complex eigenvalues are less than $1$, then the origin is an attractor and the iterates of $\textbf{x}_{0}$ spiral inward toward the origin, as in the following example.

content.heading: Survival of the Spotted Owls
content.paragraph: Recall from this chapter’s introductory example that the spotted owl population in the Willow Creek area of California was modeled by a dynamical system $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ in which the entries in $\textbf{x}_{k} = (j_{k},s_{k},a_{k})$ listed the numbers of females (at time $k$) in the juvenile, subadult, and adult life stages, respectively, and $A$ is the stage-matrix

MATLAB shows that the eigenvalues of $A$ are approximately $\text{λ}_{1} = .98$, $\text{λ}_{2} = - .02 + .21i$, and $\text{λ}_{3} = - .02 - .21i$. Observe that all three eigenvalues are less than 1 in magnitude, because $|\text{λ}_{2}|^{2} = |\text{λ}_{3}|^{2} = ( - .02)^{2} + (.21)^{2} = .0445$.

For the moment, let $A$ act on the complex vector space $\textbf{ℂ}^{3}$. Then, because $A$ has three distinct eigenvalues, the three corresponding eigenvectors are linearly independent and form a basis for $\textbf{ℂ}^{3}$. Denote the eigenvectors by $\textbf{v}_{1}$, $\textbf{v}_{2}$, and $\textbf{v}_{3}$. Then the general solution of $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ (using vectors in $\textbf{ℂ}^{3}$) has the form

If $\textbf{x}_{0}$ is a real initial vector, then $\textbf{x}_{1} = A\textbf{x}_{0}$ is real because $A$ is real. Similarly, the equation $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$ shows that each $\textbf{x}_{k}$ on the left side of (11) is real, even though it is expressed as a sum of complex vectors. However, each term on the right side of (11) is approaching the zero vector, because the eigenvalues are all less than $1$ in magnitude. Therefore the real sequence $\textbf{x}_{k}$ approaches the zero vector, too. Sadly, this model predicts that the spotted owls will eventually all perish.

Is there hope for the spotted owl? Recall from the introductory example that the $\text{18}\%~$entry in the matrix $A$ in (10) comes from the fact that although $\text{60}\%$ of the juvenile owls live long enough to leave the nest and search for new home territories, only $\text{30}\%$ of that group survive the search and find new home ranges. Search survival is strongly influenced by the number of clear-cut areas in the forest, which make the search more difficult and dangerous.

Some owl populations live in areas with few or no clear-cut areas. It may be that a larger percentage of the juvenile owls there survive and find new home ranges. Of course, the problem of the spotted owl is more complex than we have described, but the final example provides a happy ending to the story.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Suppose the search survival rate of the juvenile owls is $\text{50}\%$, so the $(2,1)\text{-entry}$ in the stage-matrix $A$ in $(10)$ is$~.3$ instead of $.18$. What does the stage-matrix model predict about this spotted owl population?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Now the eigenvalues of $A$ turn out to be approximately $\text{λ}_{1} = 1.01$, $\text{λ}_{2} = - .03 + .26i$, and $\text{λ}_{3} = - .03 - .26i$. An eigenvector for $\text{λ}_{1}$ is approximately $\textbf{v}_{1} =$ $(10,3,31)$. Let $\textbf{v}_{2}$ and $\textbf{v}_{3}$ be (complex) eigenvectors for $\text{λ}_{2}$ and $\text{λ}_{3}$. In this case, equation (11) becomes

As $k\rightarrow\text{∞}$, the second two vectors tend to zero. So $\textbf{x}_{k}$ becomes more and more like the (real) vector $c_{1}(1.01)^{k}\textbf{v}_{1}$. The approximations in equations (6) and (7), following Example 1, apply here. Also, it can be shown that the constant $c_{1}$ in the initial decomposition of $\textbf{x}_{0}$ is positive when the entries in $\textbf{x}_{0}$ are nonnegative. Thus the owl population will grow slowly, with a long-term growth rate of $1.01$. The eigenvector $\textbf{v}_{1}$ describes the eventual distribution of the owls by life stages: for every $31$ adults, there will be about $10$ juveniles and $3$ subadults.

In such a system, attractors and repellers are defined in terms of the eigenvalues of a special matrix (with variable entries) called the Jacobian matrix of the system.
